theme: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 22:1-21. This psalm will be read twice in the next two days. Today, read the first half as the voice of someone in agony, and as you read, remember that Jesus quoted its first line from the cross.
settingTheScene: Psalm 22 is attributed to David. We do not know the circumstances in which he wrote it, but the details of his suffering go far beyond anything we know of David’s life. Hands and feet pierced, bones out of joint, clothes divided by lot. The New Testament sees these words as fulfilled in Jesus. The psalm is both a real prayer of a real man and a prophecy, and that is what makes it unique. It stands next to Job as one of the great statements of the suffering of a righteous person who feels forsaken.
observation: The psalm begins, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from saving me, from the words of my groaning?” (v. 1).
He says he cries by day and by night, but there is no answer (v. 2).
Verses 3-5 turn to God’s holiness and the fact that the fathers trusted in him and were delivered.
In verse 6 he says, “But I am a worm and not a man, scorned by mankind and despised by the people.”
The crowd mocks him: “He trusts in the LORD; let him deliver him” (v. 8).
He remembers that God has been with him since birth (vv. 9-10).
Enemies surround him like bulls and lions (vv. 12-13, 16).
His body is poured out like water, his heart is like wax, and “my tongue sticks to my jaws” (vv. 14-15).
“They have pierced my hands and feet…they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots” (vv. 16-18).
He pleads, “But you, O LORD, do not be far off!” (v. 19) and “Save me from the mouth of the lion” (v. 21).
interpretation:
The most striking thing about the first line is the double name: “My God, my God.” The psalmist feels forsaken, and in that moment he does not call God by a lesser name. He calls him “my God,” twice. The sense of abandonment and the ownership of God sit side by side. This is the same paradox you saw in Job. The one who feels the most forsaken is the one who still says “my.”

Verses 3 to 5 show how the psalmist uses memory as a weapon. He says, “Yet you are holy.” He remembers that the fathers trusted God and were not put to shame. Memory is the way a person stays alive spiritually in a long night. When feeling fails, history holds.

Then the psalmist describes what it is like to be the object of contempt. “I am a worm and not a man.” The crowd’s mockery is the same sort of thing Job’s friends do, only more brutal: “He trusts in the LORD; let him deliver him.” The scorn of the crowd takes the very faith of the sufferer and turns it into a joke. That is a particular kind of pain, and the psalm gives it a name.

The physical description in verses 14 to 18 is overwhelming. And the language is so specific that the early church saw it as a portrait of the crucifixion. Crucifixion was not invented until centuries after David. Yet here are pierced hands and feet, bones out of joint, and a gambling match over clothing. The Gospels do not hide the fact that they are quoting this psalm. John 19:23-24 cites verse 18 directly.

The first half of the psalm ends in the cry of verses 19 to 21. It is still a cry. The rescue has not come yet. But the shift is already beginning, because the psalmist is asking God for help in the second person: “But you, O LORD.” The turn happens in the next verse, and you will read it tomorrow.
connection: Jesus cried Psalm 22:1 from the cross (Matthew 27:46). The mockery in verse 8 is repeated by the chief priests (Matthew 27:43). The division of garments in verse 18 is quoted in John 19:24. Hebrews 5:7 says that Jesus “offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to the one who was able to save him from death.”
application:
The next time you feel forsaken, use these words. Jesus prayed them before you, and so you are never praying alone. He knows the feeling from the inside.

Take time today to thank him for bearing the real abandonment, so that you might never be forsaken by the Father. Be specific. What did he take on himself?

If you are watching someone else suffer, do not mock their faith, even gently. Ask yourself whether a quick word of religious cheer is really a kind of mockery.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for being forsaken so that you would not be.
Tell God where you feel far from him.
Thank him that he is near now.
